## Summary

`make all` can fail during `builder-image` bootstrap on an Ubuntu 24.04 VMware host because the Ubuntu 20.04 builder image's apt HTTPS helper traps with `SIGILL` inside GnuTLS when AVX is not exposed to the guest.

## Environment

- CubeSandbox version / commit: `4166d3a`
- Host OS and kernel version: Ubuntu 24.04.2 LTS, `6.8.0-117-generic`
- KVM info (`modinfo kvm`): Not applicable; the failure happens while building the Docker builder image, before sandbox/KVM runtime is involved.
- Deployment mode: local source build / developer environment
- Relevant component: build tooling / `docker/Dockerfile.builder` / root `Makefile`

Additional host details:

```text
Docker: 29.6.1
containerd: v2.2.5
runc: 1.3.6
Virtualization: VMware
CPU: Intel Xeon Silver 4210R
```

Important CPU detail: the VMware guest exposes `aes` and `pclmulqdq`, but does not expose `avx` or `avx2`.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Use a fresh checkout on an affected Ubuntu 24.04 VMware guest.
2. Ensure no local builder image exists:

   ```bash
   docker image rm cube-sandbox-builder:ubuntu2004 || true
   ```

3. Run the documented root build path:

   ```bash
   make all
   ```

Minimal reproduction independent of CubeSandbox:

```bash
docker run --rm ubuntu:20.04 bash -lc '
  set -eux
  apt-get update -o Acquire::Retries=0
  apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends ca-certificates >/dev/null
  printf "deb https://mirrors.tencent.com/ubuntu focal main\n" >/tmp/https.list
  apt-get update -o Acquire::Retries=0 \
    -o Dir::Etc::sourcelist=/tmp/https.list \
    -o Dir::Etc::sourceparts=- \
    -o APT::Get::List-Cleanup=0
'
```

The same forced HTTPS apt source test also fails on `ubuntu:22.04`, but succeeds on `ubuntu:24.04`.

## Expected Behavior

`make all` should successfully build or bootstrap the local builder image and continue to component builds.

If a CPU feature is required by the builder path, the build should detect it explicitly and fail with a clear message. Ideally, the builder image should not implicitly require AVX.

## Actual Behavior

The build fails during builder image creation before any CubeSandbox component is built.

```text
E: Method https has died unexpectedly!
E: Sub-process https received signal 4.
make: *** [Makefile:117: builder-image] Error 1
```

The minimal reproduction fails with the same apt error:

```text
E: Method https has died unexpectedly!
E: Sub-process https received signal 4.
```

Kernel logs show that apt's HTTPS helper crashes with an illegal instruction inside GnuTLS:

```text
traps: https[...] trap invalid opcode ... in libgnutls.so.30.27.0
traps: https[...] trap invalid opcode ... in libgnutls.so.30.31.0
```

## Additional Context

Observed package versions:

```text
ubuntu:20.04: apt 2.0.10, libgnutls30 3.6.13-2ubuntu1.12
ubuntu:22.04: apt 2.4.14, libgnutls30 3.7.3-4ubuntu1.9
ubuntu:24.04: apt 2.8.3, forced HTTPS apt source succeeds
```

Disassembling the faulting offset shows the illegal instruction is AVX:

```text
vzeroupper
```

Since this VMware guest does not expose `avx`, the kernel raises `SIGILL`. apt reports that as `Sub-process https received signal 4`.

This does not appear to be "Ubuntu 24 cannot build Ubuntu 20 images" in general. It appears to be a portability issue in the builder bootstrap path: older Ubuntu apt/GnuTLS HTTPS code can enter an AVX instruction path on a VM where AVX is not available.

The builder Dockerfile appears to use HTTP for Ubuntu mirrors, but the current Tencent mirror redirects HTTP to HTTPS:

```text
HTTP/1.1 302 Found
Location: https://mirrors.tencent.com/ubuntu/dists/focal/InRelease
```

So apt may enter the HTTPS method even when the Dockerfile source URL starts with `http://`.

The LLVM install path also uses `llvm.sh`, which adds an HTTPS apt source for `apt.llvm.org`.
title: [Bug Report] builder: make all fails while building ubuntu:20.04 builder image when apt HTTPS hits GnuTLS SIGILL without AVX

body:
## Summary

Creating a template via `cubemastercli tpl create-from-image` (or the E2B build path `e2b_env_tpl.sh`) produces a rootfs artifact directory under `/usr/local/services/cubetoolbox/cubebox_os_image/rfs-<id>/` containing a ~1.1 GB `.ext4` (plus `.vm`, `version`). Deleting the template with `cubemastercli template delete` (`delete_tpl.sh`) removes the template definition and the `t_cube_rootfs_artifact` DB row, and cleans `/data/CubeMaster/storage/`, but **never deletes the `rfs-*` ext4 directory under `cubebox_os_image/`**. The orphaned 1.1 GB ext4 files accumulate indefinitely — one per built template — with no GC reclaiming them.

## Environment

- CubeSandbox version / commit: v0.3.1 `cube-sandbox-one-click-9003288`
- Host OS and kernel version: OpenCloudOS 9.4, Linux 6.6.69-1.1.cubesandbox.oc9.x86_64
- KVM info: `kvm.ko.xz` srcversion EDE4CCFC908293516155698
- Deployment mode: single-node (1/1 nodes scanned)
- Relevant component: **CubeMaster** (template/artifact lifecycle) / **Cubelet** (rootfs image storage GC)

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Create a template from an image (this is the real rootfs-producing path; `e2b_env_tpl.sh` runs `Sandbox.create(template=...)` which only consumes an existing template, the build itself is `create-from-image`):

   ```bash
   $ cubemastercli tpl create-from-image \
       --template-id tpl-9991234 \
       --image 127.0.0.1:5000/sandbox-code:latest \
       --writable-layer-size 1G \
       --expose-port 49999 --expose-port 49983 \
       --probe 49999 --cpu 500 --memory 1024
   2026/07/08 19:30:51 template_id: tpl-9991234
   2026/07/08 19:30:51 status: PENDING
   2026/07/08 19:30:51 phase: PULLING
   ```

2. Wait until READY. A new `rfs-<id>/` dir appears under `cubebox_os_image/`:

   ```bash
   $ ls -la /usr/local/services/cubetoolbox/cubebox_os_image/ | grep rfs
   drwxr-xr-x 2 root root 4096 Jul 8 19:30 rfs-b3072bcade32fdadc7b1e06c
   $ du -sh /usr/local/services/cubetoolbox/cubebox_os_image/rfs-b3072bcade32fdadc7b1e06c
   1.1G  /usr/local/services/cubetoolbox/cubebox_os_image/rfs-b3072bcade32fdadc7b1e06c
   ```

3. Delete the template (must remove all sandboxes built from it first, per `delete_tpl.sh`):

   ```bash
   $ cubemastercli template delete --template-id tpl-9991234
   2026/07/08 19:31:45 template deleted: tpl-9991234
   ```

4. Verify the template and DB record are gone:

   ```bash
   $ cubemastercli tpl ls
   TEMPLATE_ID    STATUS    CREATED_AT    IMAGE_INFO
   (no tpl-9991234)

   $ docker exec cube-sandbox-mysql mysql -ucube -pcube_pass cube_mvp -N \
       -e "SELECT artifact_id FROM t_cube_rootfs_artifact;"
   (empty — DB row deleted)

   $ ls /data/CubeMaster/storage/
   (empty — that storage path cleaned)
   ```

5. Check the rootfs dir that was created for this template:

   ```bash
   $ ls -la /usr/local/services/cubetoolbox/cubebox_os_image/ | grep rfs
   drwxr-xr-x 2 root root 4096 Jul 8 19:30 rfs-b3072bcade32fdadc7b1e06c   # <-- STILL HERE
   $ du -sh /usr/local/services/cubetoolbox/cubebox_os_image/rfs-b3072bcade32fdadc7b1e06c
   1.1G
   $ mount | grep rfs-b3072bcade32fdadc7b1e06c
   (not mounted — pure orphan file)
   ```

6. Wait >24h; the file is **not reclaimed**. (`image_expiration_time: "24h"` is configured in `Cubelet/dynamicconf/conf.yaml`, but the GC does not pick up these orphans — see Root Cause.)

## Expected Behavior

After `cubemastercli template delete` succeeds:

- Template definition removed ✅ (works)
- `t_cube_rootfs_artifact` row removed ✅ (works)
- `/data/CubeMaster/storage/rfs-<id>/` removed ✅ (works)
- **`/usr/local/services/cubetoolbox/cubebox_os_image/rfs-<id>/` removed** ❌ (NOT removed — **bug**)

The build path writes rootfs to `cubebox_os_image/`; the delete path cleans `/data/CubeMaster/storage/` but has no step that removes the `cubebox_os_image/` copy. Deletion of a template should free all storage it occupies, including the `cubebox_os_image/` rootfs artifact it was built from.

Real environment before cleanup (template count vs leaked rootfs dirs):

```
# Only one template currently exists:
$ cubemastercli tpl ls | grep -v snap-
TEMPLATE_ID     STATUS    CREATED_AT              IMAGE_INFO
tpl-500-1024    READY     2026-06-30T08:23:19Z    127.0.0.1:5000/sandbox-code:latest@sha256:b551...

# But three rootfs dirs sit on disk (each 1.1 GB):
$ ls -la /usr/local/services/cubetoolbox/cubebox_os_image/ | grep rfs
drwxr-xr-x 2 root root 4096 Jul  7 14:26 rfs-26e50e2b109b0a400ea0f8b9   # orphan (no template, no DB row)
drwxr-xr-x 2 root root 4096 Jul  1 16:52 rfs-b3072bcade32fdadc7b1e06c
drwxr-xr-x 2 root root 4096 Jul  8 17:39 rfs-b47191d4e7de7ceb02bf7179   # orphan (no template, no DB row)

$ du -sh /usr/local/services/cubetoolbox/cubebox_os_image/rfs-*
1.1G  .../rfs-26e50e2b109b0a400ea0f8b9
1.1G  .../rfs-b3072bcade32fdadc7b1e06c
1.1G  .../rfs-b47191d4e7de7ceb02bf7179

# Only ONE of these has a DB row (the one backing the surviving template):
$ docker exec cube-sandbox-mysql mysql -ucube -pcube_pass cube_mvp -N \
    -e "SELECT artifact_id,status FROM t_cube_rootfs_artifact;"
rfs-b3072bcade32fdadc7b1e06c    READY
# (rfs-26e50e2b and rfs-b47191d4 have NO DB row at all — fully orphaned)

# Full-database search for the two orphans: zero references anywhere:
rfs-...26e50e2b 全库引用: 无
rfs-...b47191d4 全库引用: 无

# None are mounted:
$ mount | grep -E 'rfs-26e50e2b|rfs-b47191d4'
(no output)
```

Fresh reproduction (create → delete, same session):

```
# Create tpl-9991234 -> produces rfs-b3072bcade (reused existing artifact, dir touched at 19:30)
# Delete tpl-9991234:
$ cubemastercli template delete --template-id tpl-9991234
template deleted: tpl-9991234

# Template gone, DB row gone, /data/CubeMaster/storage gone:
$ cubemastercli tpl ls | grep 9991234
(empty)
$ docker exec cube-sandbox-mysql mysql -ucube -pcube_pass cube_mvp -N -e "SELECT artifact_id FROM t_cube_rootfs_artifact;"
(empty)
$ ls /data/CubeMaster/storage/
(empty)

# But the rfs dir under cubebox_os_image/ is NOT removed:
$ ls /usr/local/services/cubetoolbox/cubebox_os_image/ | grep rfs
rfs-26e50e2b109b0a400ea0f8b9
rfs-b3072bcade32fdadc7b1e06c   # <-- just-deleted template's rootfs, still 1.1 GB on disk
rfs-b47191d4e7de7ceb02bf7179
# 30s later, still there; >24h later, still there.
```

Each build/delete cycle leaks ~1.1 GB. A CI/CD loop that rebuilds templates (or any workflow that creates and removes templates) will exhaust disk with unreachable ext4 files.

## Root Cause Analysis

The rootfs artifact lives in **two** places and the delete path only cleans one:

| Storage location | Written by | Cleaned by `template delete`? |
|------------------|-----------|------------------------------|
| `/data/CubeMaster/storage/rfs-<id>/*.ext4` | CubeMaster build job | ✅ Yes (removed) |
| `/usr/local/services/cubetoolbox/cubebox_os_image/rfs-<id>/*.ext4` (+ `.vm`, `version`) | Cubelet image build (ext4 rootfs for cubebox) | ❌ **No — leaked** |

`template delete` removes the `t_cube_rootfs_artifact` row and the `/data/CubeMaster/storage/` copy, but has no step that removes the `cubebox_os_image/` rootfs dir on the node. Once the DB row is deleted, the Cubelet-side GC also can no longer reclaim it — `image_expiration_time: "24h"` in `Cubelet/dynamicconf/conf.yaml` only scans rows that still exist in `t_cube_rootfs_artifact` (with a `gc_deadline`); the orphans have **no DB row to scan**, so they are permanently invisible to GC.

Evidence the orphans are unreachable by any recovery mechanism:

- **No DB row**: `t_cube_rootfs_artifact` has no entry for `rfs-26e50e2b` or `rfs-b47191d4`.
- **No reference anywhere**: full-database search across all 149 char columns in all tables finds zero matches for either orphan id.
- **Not mounted**: `mount | grep` finds nothing — these are dead files.
- **Not GC'd after >24h**: `rfs-26e50e2b` was created Jul 7 (over 24h old), still present when checked Jul 8.
- **Survives template delete in same session**: freshly-built `tpl-9991234`'s rootfs dir remains after `template delete`.

The bug: **`template delete` deletes the artifact's DB record before (or without) removing the `cubebox_os_image/` rootfs directory, and the Cubelet GC only reclaims artifacts that still have a DB row.** The two-step cleanup is not atomic/ordered, so the disk copy is stranded with no owner.

## Additional Context

- The leak is on the **root filesystem** (`/dev/vda2`, `/`), not the data disk (`/dev/vdb` → `/data/cubelet`). `cubebox_os_image/` lives under `/usr/local/services`, which is on `/`. So this leak directly consumes the usually-smaller root partition and can fill it independently of the data disk's capacity.

- `image_expiration_time: "24h"` (Cubelet dynamicconf) exists but does not cover this case — its GC scope is artifacts tracked in `t_cube_rootfs_artifact` with a `gc_deadline`. Orphans whose row is already deleted are outside that scope.

- Workaround: manually `rm -rf /usr/local/services/cubetoolbox/cubebox_os_image/rfs-<id>/` for orphans that have (a) no `t_cube_rootfs_artifact` row, (b) no `mount` entry, (c) no full-DB reference. This is what we did to reclaim 3.3 GB in the reported environment. It should not be necessary.

- Related but distinct from the snapshot-list stale-entry bug (`issue-template-list-stale-entries.md`): that one is a read-path/consistency issue (no data leak, phantom `tpl ls` entries); this one is a **real disk-space leak** (1.1 GB of unreachable ext4 per built template).

## Suggested Fix

`cubemastercli template delete` (CubeMaster) should, after removing the DB row, also issue a Cubelet-side cleanup of the `cubebox_os_image/rfs-<id>/` directory for that artifact id — or, equivalently, set the artifact's `gc_deadline` and let Cubelet GC remove the `cubebox_os_image/` copy (in addition to `/data/CubeMaster/storage/`) before/instead of deleting the row outright. The cleanup must cover both rootfs storage locations, not just `/data/CubeMaster/storage/`.
title: [Bug Report] Template delete leaks 1.1GB rootfs ext4 in cubebox_os_image (permanent disk leak, root partition exhaustion risk)

body:
## Summary
Deleted snapshot templates (`snap-*`) remain visible as `READY` in `GET /templates` (and `cubemastercli tpl ls`) indefinitely, while the same resources return `404` via `GET /templates/{id}` — a read-path inconsistency within the same API. The stale entries survive CubeMaster restarts, confirming persistent storage; they are not in MySQL, confirming the source is Cubelet's in-memory template registry pushed to CubeMaster via periodic reporting.

This is triggered by every successful snapshot deletion, including the **ephemeral snapshots created internally by `Sandbox.clone()`**. `clone()` creates a snapshot, builds N clones from it, then deletes the snapshot — and that internal `delete_snapshot` leaves a stale `snap-*` entry in the list each time. So **every clone call leaks one phantom entry**, not just explicit `create_snapshot`/`delete_snapshot` pairs.


## Environment

- CubeSandbox version / commit: v0.3.1  `cube-sandbox-one-click-9003288`
- Host OS and kernel version: OpenCloudOS 9.4, Linux 6.6.69-1.1.cubesandbox.oc9.x86_64
- KVM info: `kvm.ko.xz` srcversion EDE4CCFC908293516155698
- Deployment mode: single-node (1/1 nodes scanned)
- Relevant component: **Cubelet** (template registry reporting) / **CubeMaster** (template list aggregation)

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Create a sandbox and a snapshot inside it:

   ```python
   from cubesandbox import Sandbox

   with Sandbox.create(template="tpl-500-1024") as sb:
       sb.run_code("print('hello')")
       snap = sb.create_snapshot()
       # snap.snapshot_id == "snap-76867c25d5724d6490ef3aed" (example)
       sb.delete_snapshot(snap.snapshot_id)
   ```

2. Observe `delete_snapshot` returns success (204). The sandbox is cleaned up by `with` on exit.

3. Verify the snapshot is truly gone:

   ```bash
   $ curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' http://127.0.0.1:3000/templates/snap-76867c25d5724d6490ef3aed
   404
   ```

4. List templates:

   ```bash
   $ curl -s http://127.0.0.1:3000/templates | python3 -m json.tool
   [
     ...
     {
       "templateID": "snap-76867c25d5724d6490ef3aed",
       "status": "READY",
       "createdAt": "2026-07-08T08:23:53Z"
     }
   ]
   ```

   **The deleted snapshot still appears as `READY` in the list.**

5. Wait >8 hours; stale entries persist. Restart `cube-sandbox-cubemaster.service`; stale entries persist.

### Trigger 2 — `Sandbox.clone()` (more insidious, leaks every call)

`Sandbox.clone()` internally runs `create_snapshot` → `Sandbox.create(template=snap_id)` × n → `delete_snapshot` (see SDK docstring: "Internally this executes three steps ... 3. delete_snapshot — clean up the ephemeral snapshot"). The internal `delete_snapshot` hits the same bug, so **every clone call leaves a stale `snap-*` entry** even though the caller never touches snapshots:
```python
# clone_sandbox_by_newsb.py
from cubesandbox import Sandbox
src = Sandbox.create(template="tpl-500-1024")
src.run_code("open('/tmp/shared.txt','w').write('hello')")
clones = src.clone(n=1)          # <-- creates+deletes an ephemeral snapshot internally
for sb in clones:
    out = sb.run_code("print(open('/tmp/shared.txt').read())").logs.stdout[0]
    assert out.strip() == "hello"
# script completes successfully, exit 0; no explicit snapshot handling
```

```bash
# Before clone:
$ cubemastercli tpl ls | grep snap-
snap-2d071a...    READY @ 08:19
snap-f8025312...  READY @ 08:52

# After clone (script exit 0), a NEW stale snap appears:
$ cubemastercli tpl ls | grep snap-
snap-2d071a...    READY @ 08:19
snap-b0a4d4b3...  READY @ 09:55   # <-- leaked by this clone() call
snap-f8025312...  READY @ 08:52

# Yet the new entry is 404 on individual GET (already deleted):
$ curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' http://127.0.0.1:3000/templates/snap-b0a4d4b38a1a476099620bc2
404
```

Each additional `clone()` call accumulates one more phantom entry. A service doing fan-out cloning (e.g. the `concurrency_clone_sandbox_by_newsb.py` stress harness, or any batch agent) will pollute `tpl ls` with stale entries proportional to clone count.

## Expected Behavior

After `DELETE /templates/{id}` returns 204:

- `GET /templates/{id}` returns 404 ✅ (this works correctly)
- `GET /templates` **does not** include the deleted template (it currently does — **bug**)
- `cubemastercli tpl ls` matches API truth (it currently shows stale entries)
- `cubemastercli snapshot ls` correctly shows empty (it does ✅ — this read-path is correct)

All read paths for the same resource should agree. At minimum, the list API should invalidate its entry for a template when a successful `DELETE` is processed, or omit entries that return 404 on individual GET.


## Actual Behavior

**Trigger 1 (explicit delete_snapshot):**

```
# List says READY:
$ curl -s http://127.0.0.1:3000/templates | python3 -c '
import sys,json
d=json.load(sys.stdin)
[t for t in d if t["templateID"].startswith("snap-")]'
[{"templateID": "snap-2d071a8a2e1943a59d777a57", "status": "READY", ...},
 {"templateID": "snap-f8025312e604462a8bc89aed", "status": "READY", ...}]

# Individual GET says 404:
$ curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' http://127.0.0.1:3000/templates/snap-2d071a8a2e1943a59d777a57
404
$ curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' http://127.0.0.1:3000/templates/snap-f8025312e604462a8bc89aed
404

# Snapshot registry is correctly empty:
$ cubemastercli snapshot ls
SNAPSHOT_ID    STATUS    SANDBOX_ID    NODE_ID    CREATED_AT

# Disk is clean — no snapshot volumes remain:
$ ls /data/cubelet/storage/cubecow-reflink/volumes/ | grep snap
(no output)
```

The two stale entries above were created at 08:19 and 08:52 UTC; at 09:43 UTC (8+ hours later, after CubeMaster restart) they are still present in the list.

**Trigger 2 (clone — freshly reproduced):**

```
# Before clone:
$ cubemastercli tpl ls | grep snap-
snap-2d071a8a2e1943a59d777a57    READY    2026-07-08T08:19:04Z
snap-8ecbeb14ed19479d84a471c4    READY    2026-07-08T09:48:42Z
snap-f8025312e604462a8bc89aed    READY    2026-07-08T08:52:30Z

# After python3 clone_sandbox_by_newsb.py tpl-500-1024 (exit 0):
$ cubemastercli tpl ls | grep snap-
snap-2d071a8a2e1943a59d777a57    READY    2026-07-08T08:19:04Z
snap-8ecbeb14ed19479d84a471c4    READY    2026-07-08T09:48:42Z
snap-b0a4d4b38a1a476099620bc2    READY    2026-07-08T09:55:16Z   # <-- new phantom from clone()
snap-f8025312e604462a8bc89aed    READY    2026-07-08T08:52:30Z

# 30s later, still there (not a short TTL cache):
$ cubemastercli tpl ls | grep snap-
snap-2d071a8a2e1943a59d777a57    READY    ...
snap-8ecbeb14ed19479d84a471c4    READY    ...
snap-b0a4d4b38a1a476099620bc2    READY    ...   # <-- still
snap-f8025312e604462a8bc89aed    READY    ...

# Yet it is 404 (truly deleted):
$ curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' http://127.0.0.1:3000/templates/snap-b0a4d4b38a1a476099620bc2
404
```

Every `clone()` call accumulates one more stale entry. Over time the list becomes a graveyard of phantom snapshots that mislead operators.
## Root Cause Analysis

The inconsistency stems from a **split read-path**:

| Read path | Source | Shows deleted snapshot? |
|-----------|--------|----------------------|
| `GET /templates` (list) | CubeMaster aggregates from Cubelet periodic reports (60s interval) | ✅ **YES** (stale) |
| `GET /templates/{id}` (item) | Queries Cubelet for the specific template's backing store | ❌ No (correct 404) |
| `cubemastercli snapshot ls` | Snapshot-specific registry (different table/store) | ❌ No (correctly empty) |
| `cubemastercli tpl ls` | Same as `GET /templates` (list) | ✅ **YES** (stale) |

When `DELETE /templates/{id}` succeeds, Cubelet removes the template's backing storage (COW volume + snapshot directory) and marks it gone in the snapshot registry. However, **Cubelet's in-memory template registry** (used for the periodic `report_stat` push to CubeMaster) is **not updated** — the entry lingers. CubeMaster's list aggregation faithfully reflects what Cubelet reports, so the stale entry persists indefinitely.

Evidence the stale source is Cubelet's in-memory registry (not CubeMaster cache, not DB):

- **MySQL `cube_mvp`**: full-database search across all 149 char columns in all tables finds zero matches for the snapshot ID → not in DB.
- **Cubelet local files**: `grep -r` across `/data/cubelet` and `/usr/local/services/cubetoolbox` finds no file containing the snapshot ID → not on disk.
- **CubeMaster restart**: stale entries survive → not in CubeMaster process memory.
- **Cubelet not restarted**: `report_stat_interval=60s` keeps pushing the stale entry every minute.

The bug specifically is: **Cubelet does not remove the template entry from its in-memory registry when `DELETE /templates/{id}` is processed**, while it correctly cleans up the physical storage and snapshot-level metadata.

## Additional Context

- CubeMaster config excerpt showing the list aggregation uses Cubelet reporting, not direct DB:

  ```
  SyncMetaDataInterval    = 30000000000  (30s)
  CleanSandboxCacheInterval = 7200000000000 (2h)
  GwCacheEnable           = false
  EnabledListRunningSandboxCache = false
  ```

  None of these cache settings cover the template list path; the `CleanSandboxCacheInterval` only applies to sandbox-level caches.

- The data is **not leaked** — disk, snapshot registry, and individual GET all correctly reflect deletion. The bug is purely a **read-path consistency** issue that misleads operators into investigating phantom "leaked" snapshots.

- The bug is triggered by **every** successful `DELETE /templates/{id}`, not just explicit `delete_snapshot` calls. The most common trigger in practice is `Sandbox.clone()`, which internally creates and deletes an ephemeral snapshot on every call. Any workload doing fan-out cloning (batch agents, concurrent stress tests like `concurrency_clone_sandbox_by_newsb.py`) will accumulate stale `snap-*` entries proportional to clone count. This makes the impact far worse than a rare edge case — it is a steady leak on a frequently used API path.

- The `create_snapshot_by_tmpsb.py` and `clone_sandbox_by_newsb.py` scripts used in reproduction are standard cubesandbox SDK usage. The bug is not triggered by misuse — it reproduces on the happy path.
title: [Bug Report] Deleted snapshot templates remain in GET /templates list (list API vs single detail API data inconsistency)

body:
## Problem

Every envd data-plane call in the Go SDK (`sdk/go`) is sent to the sandbox's **Jupyter** port (`49999`) instead of the **envd** port (`49983`). Against a real deployment this makes the following fail with a non-2xx error (observed as `HTTP 404 Not Found` or `502 Bad Gateway`, depending on what the Jupyter port fronts in a given template):

- `Commands.Run` (`/process.Process/Start`)
- `Files.Read` / `Write` / `WriteFiles` (`/files`)
- `Filesystem.List` / `Stat` / `Exists` / `MakeDir` / `Rename` / `Remove` / `WatchDir` (`/filesystem.Filesystem/*`)
- `Pty` (`/process.Process/*`, added in #815)

Only `RunCode` (`/execute`) works, because `/execute` genuinely lives on the Jupyter port.

## Root Cause

The SDK only defines the Jupyter port:

```go
// sdk/go/sandbox.go
const JupyterPort = 49999
```

and `newEnvdRequest` — the shared builder for **all** envd RPCs (process, files, filesystem) — hardcodes it as the host port:

```go
// sdk/go/envd.go
func (s *Sandbox) newEnvdRequest(ctx context.Context, method, path string, query url.Values, body io.Reader) (*http.Request, error) {
	target := url.URL{
		Scheme: s.client.config.ProxyScheme,
		Host:   s.GetHost(JupyterPort), // <-- should be the envd port (49983)
		Path:   path,
		...
	}
}
```

CubeProxy routes by the port prefix in the virtual host (`<port>-<sandboxID>.<domain>`), so these requests are forwarded to the Jupyter kernel gateway, which does not serve `/process.Process/*`, `/files`, or `/filesystem.Filesystem/*` → non-2xx (404 or 502).

## Evidence (live run)

Against a real CubeSandbox (`api=http://127.0.0.1:13000`, `proxy=127.0.0.1:11080`, `domain=cube.app`), with the proxy DNS-bypassed via `ProxyNodeIP`.

**1) Existing `Commands.Run` integration test — 404 on port 49999 (template `tpl-58f2b99af8684ca48973a61b`):**

```
=== RUN   TestIntegrationSandboxExecutionCommandsFilesAndErrors
    integration_test.go:57: CubeSandbox integration target api=http://127.0.0.1:13000 template=tpl-58f2b99af8684ca48973a61b proxy=127.0.0.1:11080 domain=cube.app
    integration_test.go:150: Commands.Run returned error: Not Found (HTTP 404)
--- FAIL: TestIntegrationSandboxExecutionCommandsFilesAndErrors (2.62s)
```

(Note: `RunCode` at line 90 — `/execute` on 49999 — succeeded; the failure is the first `/process.Process/*` call.)

**2) PTY E2E — same 404 on port 49999:**

```
=== RUN   TestIntegrationPtyLifecycle
    pty_integration_test.go:60: CubeSandbox integration target api=http://127.0.0.1:13000 template=tpl-58f2b99af8684ca48973a61b proxy=127.0.0.1:11080 domain=cube.app
    pty_integration_test.go:80: pty.Create returned error: Not Found (HTTP 404)
--- FAIL: TestIntegrationPtyLifecycle (1.40s)
```

**3) After pointing `newEnvdRequest` at the envd port `49983` — full PTY lifecycle passes (create → echo → resize/`stty size` → reattach → kill):**

```
=== RUN   TestIntegrationPtyLifecycle
    pty_integration_test.go:60: CubeSandbox integration target api=http://127.0.0.1:13000 template=tpl-58f2b99af8684ca48973a61b proxy=127.0.0.1:11080 domain=cube.app
    pty_integration_test.go:82: PTY started, pid=27
    pty_integration_test.go:131: reattached.Wait -> code=-1 err=PTY exited with error: signal: killed exitKnown=true endErr="signal: killed"
    pty_integration_test.go:141: second Kill correctly reported not-found (false)
--- PASS: TestIntegrationPtyLifecycle (1.74s)
PASS
ok  	github.com/tencentcloud/CubeSandbox/sdk/go	1.742s
```

Same `api`/`proxy`/`template`; the **only** change between runs #2 and #3 was `GetHost(JupyterPort)` → `GetHost(49983)` in `newEnvdRequest`.

**4) Same-sandbox A/B (raw HTTP, only the host port differs), template `tpl-d635607121a94ef5b9413339`:**

```
GET /files @49999 -> HTTP 502 (openresty "Bad Gateway")
GET /files @49983 -> HTTP 200, body = /etc/hostname contents
```

Identical request; flipping the virtual-host port prefix from `49999` to `49983` is the only change, and it flips failure → success. (This template returns `502` where the one in runs #1–#3 returned `404` — the failure code depends on the Jupyter upstream, but the wrong-port routing is the same bug.)

## Cross-SDK parity

Python and Node both keep the two ports separate:

- Python: `ENVD_PORT = 49983` (`_commands.py`) for process/filesystem; `JUPYTER_PORT = 49999` (`sandbox.py`) for `/execute`.
- Node: `ENVD_PORT = 49983` (`commands.ts`) for process/pty; `JUPYTER_PORT = 49999` (`sandbox.ts`) for `/execute`.

The architecture docs also state envd is health-probed on `:49983`.

## Impact

All data-plane envd functionality of the Go SDK (commands, files, filesystem, and PTY) is unusable against real deployments. Existing unit tests do not catch this: they route through a single `httptest` server via `ProxyNodeIP`, so the virtual host's port prefix never selects a backend and the wrong port is never exercised.

## Proposed Solution

1. Add `const EnvdPort = 49983`.
2. In `newEnvdRequest`, use `s.GetHost(EnvdPort)` (process/files/filesystem).
3. Leave `RunCode`'s `/execute` on `JupyterPort` (49999).
4. Add an integration-tagged E2E (or extend the existing one) that actually drives `Commands.Run`/`Files`/`Pty` against a live sandbox so the port is covered.

This is a one-line routing fix; every `newEnvdRequest`-based API (including the PTY added in #815) recovers automatically.
title: [Bug Report] Go SDK sends envd data-plane RPCs to the Jupyter port (49999) instead of envd (49983)

body:
## Summary

With more than one CubeProxy replica, the **first request to a sandbox after it auto-pauses intermittently returns 504** (~3s) and fails to trigger auto-resume; the sandbox stays paused. The failure probability is ~`(N-1)/N` for `N` replicas.

## Environment

- CubeSandbox version / commit: `master` (verified on current HEAD; the relevant code paths are unchanged in `release-0.5.x`)
- Host OS and kernel version: N/A — this is a control-plane request-routing bug, independent of host/KVM
- KVM info (`modinfo kvm`): N/A
- Deployment mode: cluster, **CubeProxy with replicas ≥ 2** behind a load balancer / Ingress that spreads traffic across pod endpoints (not sandbox-sticky)
- Relevant component: **CubeProxy** (lua gate) + **cube-lifecycle-manager** (auto-pause/resume sidecar)

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Deploy CubeProxy with `replicas: 2` (each pod runs its own co-located `cube-lifecycle-manager`), fronted by a load balancer that round-robins across the pod endpoints.
2. Create a sandbox with auto-pause + auto-resume enabled; start a listener inside it and note its proxied host.
3. Leave it idle until it auto-pauses (confirm the sandbox reaches `paused`).
4. Send the **first** request to the sandbox host.

To make it deterministic, bypass the LB and send the same first request directly to each replica's dataplane listener:
- Request to the **replica that consumed this sandbox's lifecycle events** → `200`, sandbox resumes.
- Request to **any other replica** → `504` after ~3s, and the sandbox **stays paused** (no resume attempted).

## Expected Behavior

The first request after auto-pause transparently resumes the sandbox and returns `200`, regardless of replica count or which replica serves the request.

## Actual Behavior

With `N` CubeProxy replicas, the first post-pause request has a `~(N-1)/N` chance of returning `504` after ~3s (nginx `proxy_connect_timeout`) and leaving the sandbox paused. Subsequent requests may succeed once some request happens to land on the owning replica and resumes it.

```
first request -> non-owning replica: HTTP 504 in 3.01s, sandbox still "paused"
first request -> owning replica:     HTTP 200 in 0.10s, sandbox -> "running"
```

## Root Cause

The auto-pause/resume state is **per-replica** and is fed by a **competing-consumer** partition of the lifecycle event stream, so only one replica ever learns about a given sandbox:

1. CubeMaster publishes sandbox lifecycle `create`/`delete` events to a Redis Stream (`cube:v1:shared:sandbox:lifecycle:events`) plus a meta `HSet` snapshot (`…:lifecycle:meta`).
2. Every `cube-lifecycle-manager` consumes that stream with a **fixed shared consumer group** `"cube-proxy-sidecar"` (`cube-lifecycle-manager/internal/config/config.go:101`) and a per-host consumer name. Redis Stream consumer-group semantics = **competing consumers**: each event is delivered to **exactly one** replica (`cube-lifecycle-manager/internal/redisstream/stream.go:88`, `XReadGroup Streams=[key, ">"]`).
3. That single replica applies the event only to (a) its **in-memory registry** and (b) its **co-located** nginx admin dict over loopback (`127.0.0.1:8082`). There is no cross-replica propagation, so the other replicas' `cube_sandbox_state` dicts never learn the sandbox exists.
4. The lua gate reads the **per-replica** shared dict on the hot path and treats a **dict MISS as "running → pass through"** (`CubeProxy/lua/sandbox_state.lua:47`, `if not state or state == "running" then return end`). So a first post-pause request routed to a non-owning replica bypasses the resume gate; nginx `proxy_pass` dials the vCPU-frozen guest, the SYN is black-holed, and `proxy_connect_timeout 3s` fires → **504**. It also never fires `/_sidecar_resume`, so that request does not wake the sandbox.
5. Even forcing a miss through `/_sidecar_resume` on a non-owning replica does not help as-is: the resumer requires the sandbox in the **local** in-memory registry (`cube-lifecycle-manager/internal/resumer/resumer.go`, `doResume` → `"sandbox not in registry"`), which the non-owning replica also lacks.

The intermittency (~`(N-1)/N`) is purely a function of which replica the load balancer picks for the first request.

## Proposed Fixes

**Workaround (zero code):** run CubeProxy with `replicas: 1`. Eliminates cross-replica divergence. Cost: no CubeProxy HA.

**Real fix — fan out lifecycle events so every replica holds full state.** Cross-replica pause/resume is *already* serialized by the shared Redis `SETNX` state lock (`AcquireState` on `…:lifecycle:state:<id>`), so having every replica consume every event is safe. Two ways:

- **(a) per-replica unique consumer group** — every replica receives all events. Downside: orphan consumer groups accumulate in Redis on pod churn and need periodic `XGROUP DESTROY` cleanup.
- **(b) groupless `XREAD` (preferred)** — each replica reads the whole stream from its own in-memory cursor; no consumer groups, nothing to clean up. This fits the existing design: the meta `HSet` is the authoritative snapshot (already loaded via `HGETALL` bootstrap at startup) and the stream is a delta feed, so the group's at-least-once/PEL/redelivery guarantees are unnecessary. (To avoid a startup gap, record the stream's current last-ID before the bootstrap `HGETALL`, then `XREAD` from that ID.)

**Alternative (keeps competing consumption, serving-side authority):** on a local dict MISS, have the gate consult the shared Redis state key instead of passing through, **and** have the resumer fall back to the shared meta `HSet` when the sandbox is absent from the local registry. More moving parts (a Redis client inside OpenResty, plus Redis credentials in the nginx config).

## Additional Context

Related but distinct: #790 (auto-resume recovery after node failure) and #793 (autopause activity signals). This report is specifically about **per-replica state visibility under a shared consumer group**, which is orthogonal to those.

Happy to submit a PR for the groupless `XREAD` fix (option b) if the maintainers agree with the direction.
title: [Bug Report] Multi-replica CubeProxy: first request after auto-pause intermittently 504s (per-replica auto-resume state visibility)

body:
## Problem / Motivation

The Go SDK (`sdk/go`) has no PTY (pseudo-terminal) support, so Go users cannot run interactive programs that require a real TTY — shells/REPLs, full-screen tools (`vim`, `top`, `htop`), or agent-driven interactive terminals — against a sandbox.

This is also a cross-SDK parity gap:

- **Python** — has `sandbox.pty` (added in #579, `cubesandbox/_pty.py`).
- **Node.js** — adds `sandbox.pty` in #792 (`sdk/node/src/pty.ts`).
- **Go** — no PTY API. `sdk/go/envd.go` only defines a `PTY` data-event field for parsing stream output; there is no way to *start* or *drive* a PTY.

Anyone building Go agents/tools on CubeSandbox is currently forced to drop to raw `process.Process` Connect calls by hand, or switch languages, to get interactive terminal behavior.

## Proposed Solution

Add a `sandbox.Pty()` namespace to the Go SDK mirroring the Python/Node surface:

```go
type PtySize struct{ Rows, Cols int }

// Streaming RPCs
Create(ctx context.Context, size PtySize, opts ...PtyOption) (*PtyHandle, error) // /process.Process/Start
Connect(ctx context.Context, pid int, opts ...PtyOption) (*PtyHandle, error)     // /process.Process/Connect

// Unary selector RPCs
Kill(ctx context.Context, pid int) (bool, error)                 // /process.Process/SendSignal (SIGNAL_SIGKILL)
SendStdin(ctx context.Context, pid int, data []byte) error       // /process.Process/SendInput
Resize(ctx context.Context, pid int, size PtySize) error         // /process.Process/Update
```

`PtyHandle` exposes:
- streamed raw output (e.g. an output channel / iterator),
- `Wait() (int, error)` → exit code (surfacing envd's end-event error, e.g. `signal: killed`),
- `Disconnect()` (detach without killing; reattach later via `Connect`),
- per-handle `Kill()` / `SendStdin()` / `Resize()`,
- `Pid` / `ExitCode` / `Error`.

Behavior to match Python/Node:
- `Create` starts `/bin/bash -i -l` with a `pty.size`, seeding `TERM=xterm-256color`, `LANG=C.UTF-8`, `LC_ALL=C.UTF-8` (caller-overridable).
- `Kill` returns `false` (not error) on Connect `not_found` / HTTP 404.
- `timeout` sent to envd as `Connect-Timeout-Ms` plus a client-side idle abort.

Wire protocol (already used by `commands.Run`):
- Streaming `Start` / `Connect` over `application/connect+json` (5-byte envelope framing).
- Unary `SendSignal` / `SendInput` / `Update` over `application/json`.
- protobuf `bytes` fields (`input.pty`, `data.pty`) are base64 on the JSON side.

## Additional Context

- Python implementation: #579 (`sdk/python/cubesandbox/_pty.py`)
- Node.js implementation: #792 (`sdk/node/src/pty.ts`) — includes unit tests and live E2E (create → sendStdin/echo → resize with `stty size` readback → connect-reattach → kill).
- Go today already parses the `pty` data field (`sdk/go/envd.go`), so only the request/selector side and a `PtyHandle` need to be added.

body:
## Problem / Motivation

We run long-lived agents inside CubeSandbox VMs through the E2B-compatible API. In this pattern, sandbox lifetime and template freshness are part of the correctness boundary, not just operational details.

Two gaps make incidents hard to prevent and diagnose:

1. Sandbox lease / timeout state is not easy to verify or renew deterministically from the host side. A sandbox may be reused across runs, but a create-time `timeout` can behave like a fixed lease unless the client explicitly renews it. For agent-in-sandbox workloads, long LLM calls, builds, or outbound-only work may produce little or no ingress traffic, so the host needs a clear renewal contract and an observable `endAt`/deadline before starting each run.
2. Template / runner drift is hard to detect. A custom template can pass platform compatibility checks while the application-level runner baked into the image is stale. If the CubeSandbox guest version and SDK/runtime version are unchanged, a host-side hello check cannot distinguish the new template from an old one unless it shells into the sandbox and hashes files manually.

The result is that a stale template or an unrenewed sandbox lease can pass preflight checks and only fail during a long agent run.

Related: #793 covers richer activity signals beyond ingress traffic for autopause. This request is narrower and complementary: expose deterministic lease metadata/renewal and template provenance so orchestrators can fail fast before starting work.

## Proposed Solution

### 1. Template and sandbox provenance metadata

Please support user-defined labels/annotations on templates, and expose both user-defined and platform-generated provenance in template and sandbox detail APIs.

Useful fields include:

- template id
- template artifact/snapshot id
- source image digest
- guest image version and digest
- cube-agent / envd version
- template build timestamp
- arbitrary user labels, for example `runner_sha256`, `runner_build_id`, `app_version`

The same metadata should be visible after `Sandbox.create`, or available through a sandbox detail endpoint, so a host can reject stale templates before launching the workload.

### 2. Explicit lease renewal / deadline visibility

Please document and expose the effective sandbox deadline in the E2B-compatible API:

- current `endAt` / pause deadline on sandbox create/detail/list
- an explicit `setTimeout` / renew lease operation that updates that deadline
- SDK-level helper semantics, if the E2B-compatible SDK already supports this operation

The important property is: before each long run, the host can renew the sandbox lease, read back the new deadline, and know the sandbox will not expire before the run-level timeout unless another failure happens.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A client can create a template with labels such as `runner_sha256=<sha>` and later read the same label through template/sandbox metadata without entering the VM.
- Template/sandbox metadata includes enough automatic provenance to distinguish two app image builds that share the same CubeSandbox guest version.
- A client can renew a sandbox lease before a long run, then read back an updated `endAt`/deadline.
- Current behavior remains backward compatible for users who do not set labels or renew leases.

## Additional Context

This comes from operating CubeSandbox v0.4.0 with custom agent images and long-running agent workloads. The issue is not specific to one application runner: any agent platform that bakes a frequently changing runner into a CubeSandbox template needs a host-visible provenance contract, and any long-running in-VM workload benefits from deterministic lease renewal.
title: [Bug Report] Long-running agent sandboxes lack host-visible lease and template freshness guarantees

body:
## Summary

Domain-based CubeEgress / Credential Vault rules can fail when the sandbox DNS path returns A records with `TTL=0`.

In this case CubeVS learns the domain's A record into `allow_out_v2` with `L7_REQUIRED`, but the learned entry expires immediately. The subsequent TCP/443 connection can no longer match the L7-marked IP entry, so the traffic never reaches CubeEgress. The same Credential Vault injection works when a static IPv4 L7 target is configured.

## Environment

- CubeSandbox version / commit:
  - one-click package: `release_version=v0.4.0`
  - package commit: `4004a6ec34a9d045a9789a1fd438d6518eedb3d3`
- CubeEgress health:
  - `{"commit":"56484984","version":"v1.0.0","build_time":"20260629","bootstrap_status":"ready","policy_count":0,"status":"ok"}`
- Host OS and kernel version:
  - `Linux lex-mini-2604 5.15.0-179-generic #189-Ubuntu SMP Tue May 5 18:20:56 UTC 2026 x86_64 GNU/Linux`
- KVM info (`modinfo kvm`):
  - `filename: /lib/modules/5.15.0-179-generic/kernel/arch/x86/kvm/kvm.ko`
  - `name: kvm`
- Deployment mode:
  - single-node one-click deployment
- Relevant component:
  - CubeNet / CubeVS, network-agent, CubeEgress

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Use a template that trusts the CubeEgress root CA.

2. Create a sandbox with `allow_internet_access=False` and a domain-based L7 rule with credential injection:

   ```python
   from cubesandbox import Sandbox, Rule, Match, Action, Inject

   rules = [
       Rule(
           name="openai_inject",
           match=Match(
               scheme="https",
               host="api.openai.com",
               path="/v1/models",
           ),
           action=Action(
               allow=True,
               audit="full",
               inject=[
                   Inject(
                       header="Authorization",
                       format="Bearer ${SECRET}",
                       secret="<redacted>",
                   ),
               ],
           ),
       ),
   ]

   Sandbox.create(
       template="<template-with-cubeegress-ca>",
       allow_internet_access=False,
       network={"rules": rules},
   )
   ```

3. From inside the sandbox, query DNS through the sandbox resolver:

   ```text
   resolvers=['119.29.29.29']
   api.openai.com=[
     {'ip': '172.66.0.243', 'ttl': 0},
     {'ip': '162.159.140.245', 'ttl': 0}
   ]
   ```

4. Run:

   ```bash
   curl -sS -m 20 https://api.openai.com/v1/models
   ```

## Expected Behavior

Domain-based L7 rules should reliably route matching TCP/443 traffic to CubeEgress after the sandbox resolves the configured domain, even if the DNS response TTL is `0` or very short.

Once a TCP connection has been classified as L7-required and redirected to CubeEgress, the same connection should keep using the CubeEgress path until FIN/RST or an idle timeout, instead of depending on the DNS-learned entry still being unexpired for every later packet.

## Actual Behavior

The domain-only L7 rule fails before the request reaches CubeEgress:

```text
curl: (7) Failed to connect to api.openai.com port 443 after 205 ms: Couldn't connect to server
curl_http=000 remote=
curl_exit=7
```

The same behavior was reproduced with other domains that also returned `TTL=0` through the sandbox resolver:

```text
litellm.local.lexmount.net=[{'ip': '10.2.62.142', 'ttl': 0}]
httpbingo.org=[{'ip': '66.241.125.232', 'ttl': 0}]
www.baidu.com=[{'cname_ttl': 0}, {'ip': '110.242.70.57', 'ttl': 0}, {'ip': '110.242.69.21', 'ttl': 0}]
```

For comparison, adding a static IPv4 L7 target for the same destination makes the request reach CubeEgress and the upstream service:

```python
rules = [
    Rule(
        name="openai_static_target",
        match=Match(scheme="https", host="172.66.0.243"),
        action=Action(allow=True, audit="metadata"),
    ),
    Rule(
        name="openai_inject",
        match=Match(scheme="https", host="api.openai.com", path="/v1/models"),
        action=Action(
            allow=True,
            audit="full",
            inject=[
                Inject(
                    header="Authorization",
                    format="Bearer ${SECRET}",
                    secret="<redacted-test-key>",
                ),
            ],
        ),
    ),
]
```

With `curl --resolve api.openai.com:443:172.66.0.243 https://api.openai.com/v1/models`, the sandbox receives an upstream OpenAI response:

```text
curl_http=401 remote=172.66.0.243
{
  "error": {
    "message": "Incorrect API key provided: sk-cube-************-use. ...",
    "type": "invalid_request_error",
    "code": "invalid_api_key"
  }
}
```

This confirms that:

- the template trusts the CubeEgress CA;
- CubeEgress credential injection itself works;
- the failure is in the domain-based CubeVS DNS-learned L7 routing path.

## Root Cause

The current DNS-learning path appears to use the DNS TTL directly as the lifetime of the learned L7 IP entry:

- `CubeNet/src/dns_response.h`
  - `dns_learn_response_ip()` sets:
    - `expires_at_ns = bpf_ktime_get_ns() + ((__u64)ttl * NSEC_PER_SEC)`
- `CubeNet/src/mvmtap.bpf.c`
  - `check_net_policy()` only treats an `allow_out_v2` entry as matched when `expires_at_ns == 0 || expires_at_ns > now`
  - `should_redirect_to_l7_proxy()` only redirects TCP/80 and TCP/443 when the matched policy value has `NET_POLICY_FLAG_L7_REQUIRED`

When `ttl == 0`, the learned L7 entry is immediately expired. The TCP SYN that follows the DNS response no longer has a valid L7-marked `allow_out_v2` entry, so it is not redirected to CubeEgress.

There is a related long-connection concern: if the DNS TTL is non-zero but shorter than a long-lived HTTP stream / WebSocket / keep-alive connection, later packets may stop matching the DNS-learned L7 entry after expiration unless CubeVS pins the L7 decision per TCP flow.

## Suggested Direction

Two changes seem necessary to make Credential Vault / CubeEgress domain rules robust:

1. Apply a minimum effective TTL for DNS-learned L7 entries.

   For example:

   ```text
   effective_ttl = max(dns_ttl, 30)
   ```

   This could be limited to `L7_REQUIRED` entries or made configurable.

2. Add TCP L7 flow pinning.

   Once the initial TCP SYN matches an `L7_REQUIRED` destination and is redirected to CubeEgress, remember that 5-tuple and keep redirecting subsequent packets of the same connection to CubeEgress until FIN/RST or idle timeout. DNS TTL should decide whether a new connection can be classified, not whether an already-classified connection keeps its L7 path.

Additional considerations:

- fail closed if CubeEgress is unavailable, rather than bypassing credential injection;
- expose learned DNS entries and L7-pinned flows through `cubevsmapdump` for debugging;
- keep CubeEgress responsible for per-request Host/SNI/path/method allow/deny/inject decisions, so flow pinning is only a routing decision and not an authorization result.

## Additional Context

This issue is specific to HTTPS Credential Vault / CubeEgress domain rules. Plain HTTP credential injection is currently not covered by this report.

Static IPv4/CIDR L7 targets can be used as a workaround for fixed upstream services, but this is not a good long-term solution for CDN-backed services such as `api.openai.com`.

body:
## Problem / Motivation

Autopause decides whether a sandbox is idle using a single signal: completed inbound requests through CubeProxy. The idle check is idleFor = now - max(LastActiveMs, CreatedAt), and once idleFor >= timeout the sandbox is paused.
  
This works well for the classic request/response pattern (user → sandbox → response → wait). But it misjudges agent-in-sandbox (such as openclaw, claude-code and hermes...) workloads, where the agent runs inside the VM and does most of its work without any inbound proxy traffic:
 
- An agent busy computing, running a build, or doing a long local task generates zero ingress requests — it looks idle and gets paused mid-task.
- An agent whose only network activity is outbound (calling an LLM API, fetching resources, pushing to a remote) also generates no ingress — same misjudgment.

When such a sandbox is paused, its outbound TCP connections are dropped, stalling the in-flight work. The agent effectively gets killed for being "idle" while it was actively working.

The root issue: ingress traffic is a proxy for activity, but for agent-in-sandbox it's the wrong proxy. There's currently no way for a workload to tell the platform "I'm still busy" other than sending itself dummy inbound requests or setting an impractically large timeout. This pattern is becoming central as more workloads run the agent inside the sandbox, and current activity detection is structurally unsuited to it.


## Proposed Solution

Let autopause consider additional activity signals beyond ingress traffic, configurable per sandbox. The idle baseline would become the most recent timestamp across any enabled signal (a sandbox is idle only when all its enabled signals are quiet):

- In-VM activity (CPU / load) — the sandbox is doing real work locally.
- Egress activity — the sandbox is making outbound calls.
- Agent heartbeat — the workload explicitly reports liveness.

This keeps the current behavior as the default (ingress-only) and is fully backward compatible: a sandbox that doesn't opt into extra signals behaves exactly as today.

The exact configuration surface and which signals to support first are open for discussion — the goal of this issue is to agree that ingress-only detection is insufficient for agent-in-sandbox, and the detection should be extensible.

## Additional Context
- Current mechanism: CubeProxy/lua/log_phase.lua (activity stamp) → sidecar /admin/last_active poll → CubeProxy/sidecar/internal/sweeper/sweeper.go (sweepOnce, baseline = max(LastActiveMs, CreatedAt)).
- Prior art: e2b's lifecycle model (https://e2b.dev/docs/sandbox/auto-resume) similarly relies on timeout + explicit setTimeout renewal and has no in-VM / egress activity detection. This proposal is an extension beyond that model, targeting the agent-in-sandbox use case that ingress-based detection does not cover.
title: [Feature Request] Support activity signals beyond ingress traffic for autopause

body:
## Summary

A sandbox that was automatically paused (on_timeout="pause" + auto_resume=true) cannot be resumed after its host node fails, because the auto-pause memory snapshot is node-local and resume is hard-routed back to the original node — the in-memory state is lost and the client is left retrying a 503 forever.


## Environment

  - CubeSandbox version / commit: master @ 0894ee7
  - Host OS and kernel version: Alibaba Cloud Linux 3 (Soaring Falcon); kernel 7.0.2-1.el8.elrepo.x86_64
  - KVM info (modinfo kvm): kvm.ko vermagic 7.0.2-1.el8.elrepo.x86_64 
  - Deployment mode: cluster (multi-node)
  - Relevant component: CubeMaster / Cubelet / CubeShim / CubeProxy (+ sidecar)

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Create a sandbox with auto-pause enabled:
  sb = Sandbox.create(
      template="<tpl>",
      timeout=300,
      lifecycle={"on_timeout": "pause", "auto_resume": True},
  )
2. Let it idle past timeout so the platform auto-pauses it. The VM is frozen in place on its host (node A) and state becomes paused.
3. Take node A down (crash / power loss / network partition / disk failure).
4. Send any request to the sandbox to trigger auto-resume (e.g. run_code, HTTP to getHost()).

## Expected Behavior

  Either:
  - the request transparently resumes the sandbox (true HA / cross-node resume), or
  - if recovery is impossible, the platform fails fast with a non-retriable status (e.g. 410 Gone), converges the sandbox to a clear terminal state, and stops clients from retrying indefinitely.
  
  The failure domain of auto-pause should also be documented so users don't mistake it for a high-availability pause.

## Actual Behavior

The client receives a retriable 503 + Retry-After, but retries never succeed because the memory snapshot lives only on the dead node. The sandbox stays stuck in paused until the idle sweeper eventually tries to kill it (which itself must reach node A's cubelet, so it resolves only via NotFound/timeout + registry eviction). The in-memory state is permanently lost.
title: Auto-resume cannot recover a paused sandbox after node failure

Problem / Motivation
While exploring automation for PR routing, we prototyped a workflow that would:

Parse changed files against .github/CODEOWNERS
Post a PR comment summarizing affected modules
Auto-assign suggested code owners
Request reviews from those owners
Maintainers noted that similar functionality already exists in this repository. From a contributor’s perspective, however, it is not obvious which parts are already covered natively by GitHub vs. by existing CubeSandbox automation, and what (if anything) is still missing.

This makes it easy to propose duplicate CI work and hard for new contributors to understand how PR ownership and review routing are supposed to work.

Context
The prototype added:

.github/workflows/pr-auto-triage.yml
.github/scripts/pr_module_triage.py
Branch (fork, not merged): ls-ggg:feat/pr-auto-triage

Related existing pieces we are aware of:

.github/CODEOWNERS — module ownership rules (refreshed in #771)
.github/workflows/code-review.yml — Claude auto review on PR open/sync (pull_request_target)
.github/workflows/issue-triage.yml — issue label triage (not PR module routing)
Native GitHub CODEOWNERS review requests (when branch protection / code owner review is enabled)
Proposed Solution
Please document (or point to existing docs for) the canonical PR triage flow for CubeSandbox:

How module ownership is determined from CODEOWNERS
Whether assignees and/or reviewers are set automatically today
Whether a module summary comment is expected or desired, or intentionally out of scope
How this interacts with code-review.yml and other bots (e.g. cubesandboxbot)
If the existing setup already covers assign/review routing, it would help to state that explicitly in contributor docs so duplicate workflows are not reintroduced.

Alternatives Considered
Land the prototype pr-auto-triage workflow — deferred after maintainer feedback that overlap exists
Rely only on native GitHub CODEOWNERS — works for review requests, but does not document module summaries or assignee behavior
Additional Context
Happy to close or abandon the prototype branch if maintainers confirm the current flow is sufficient. A short maintainer reply mapping “existing feature → file/workflow” would be enough to unblock us.

body:
## Problem / Motivation

CubeSandbox is positioned as an E2B-compatible sandbox service for AI agents, and the repository already provides first-party SDKs under `sdk/`, including Python and Go.

Many AI agent applications are built in Node.js / TypeScript ecosystems, such as Next.js, LangChain.js, Vercel AI SDK, NestJS, and serverless workers. Today, Node.js developers need to either call the REST/OpenAPI API manually or try to adapt the E2B JavaScript SDK. This works for basic compatibility, but it makes CubeSandbox-specific capabilities harder to discover and use consistently.

A first-party Node.js / TypeScript SDK would lower adoption friction for JavaScript developers and make CubeSandbox easier to integrate into production agent platforms.

## Proposed Solution

Add an official Node.js / TypeScript SDK, for example under `sdk/node`, published to npm as something like `@cubesandbox/sdk`.

Suggested API shape:

```ts
import { Sandbox } from '@cubesandbox/sdk'

const sandbox = await Sandbox.create({
  apiUrl: process.env.CUBE_API_URL,
  templateId: process.env.CUBE_TEMPLATE_ID,
  proxyNodeIp: process.env.CUBE_PROXY_NODE_IP,
})

const result = await sandbox.runCode('x = 1; x + 1', {
  language: 'python',
  timeout: 10_000,
  onStdout: (msg) => console.log(msg.text),
  onStderr: (msg) => console.error(msg.text),
})

console.log(result.text)

const cmd = await sandbox.commands.run('echo hello cube')
console.log(cmd.stdout)

## Description

`cubemastercli template create` fails with `MissingMemoryZones` on AMD Strix Halo (8060S, 93GB RAM single NUMA node). CubeAPI template creation works fine because it uses a different endpoint.

## Environment

| Item | Value |
|------|-------|
| CubeSandbox | v0.5.0 |
| containerd-shim-cube-rs | v0.5.0 (30b4e25) |
| Host | Fedora 44, AMD Strix Halo (8060S) |
| RAM | 93GB, single NUMA node 0 |
| Memory zones | DMA(4MB managed), DMA32(1.6GB managed), Normal(94GB managed) |

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Use cubemastercli to create a template:
```json
{
  "template_id": "tpl-test",
  "instance_type": "cubebox",
  "volumes": [{
    "name": "tmp",
    "volume_source": {
      "empty_dir": {"medium": 0, "size_limit": "10G"}
    }
  }],
  "containers": [{
    "name": "cubebox-default",
    "image": {"image": "cube-sandbox-cn.tencentcloudcr.com/cube-sandbox/sandbox-code:latest"},
    "resources": {"cpu": "2", "mem": "2000"},
    "volume_mounts": [{"name": "tmp", "container_path": "/"}],
    "security_context": {"privileged": true}
  }]
}
```

2. Run:
```bash
sudo cubemastercli template create -f template.json
```

## Actual Result

```
Error: template creation failed: failed to run container: failed to create shim task: 
Others("Other: Create sandbox failed:Boot vm failed:Memory manager error: MissingMemoryZones, status: launched")
```

## Root Cause Analysis

cubemastercli uses `/cube/template` API endpoint which boots a Firecracker VM to create the template snapshot. The VM's memory manager (`containerd-shim-cube-rs`) can't find expected memory zones on AMD Strix Halo's single-NUMA memory layout.

CubeAPI creates templates via `/cube/template/from-image` endpoint, which creates snapshots directly from pulled images without booting a VM — this path works fine.

## Expected Behavior

cubemastercli's Firecracker shim should handle non-standard NUMA/memory-zone layouts, or fall back gracefully.
title: cubemastercli template create fails with MissingMemoryZones on AMD Strix Halo

## Bug Description

When `DisableHostCgroup` is set to `false` in cubelet config, sandbox creation fails:

```
set cubebox cgroup limit error: write /sys/fs/cgroup/cube_sandbox/sandbox/3/cpu.max: invalid argument
```

When `DisableHostCgroup` is `true`, sandboxes work but without any CPU/memory resource limits.

## Root Cause

Two issues:
1. The cubelet writes incorrect value format to cgroup v2 `cpu.max` (should be `$MAX $PERIOD`, e.g., `200000 100000` for 2 CPU)
2. The sandbox agent (Rust) tries to use cgroup v1 path `cpu.cfs_quota_us` which doesn't exist on cgroup v2-only systems

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Set `disable_host_cgroup: false` in cubelet dynamicconf
2. Restart cubelet
3. Create a sandbox → fails with "write cpu.max: invalid argument"

## Environment

- Cube Sandbox: v0.5.0 (self-compiled with controller fix)
- OS: Fedora 44, Linux 7.0.13, x86_64
- cgroup: v2 only (cgroup2fs)
- Installation: bare-metal one-click

## Impact

- With `true`: no resource isolation (sandboxes can use unlimited CPU/RAM)
- With `false`: sandbox creation fails entirely

## Workaround

Set `disable_host_cgroup: true` — sandboxes work but without resource limits.

Related: #750, #751

## Bug Description

Cubelet crashes approximately every 5 minutes:

```
LogLevel: FATAL
LogContent: controller run-template-manager is not a valid CubeMetaController
```

This happens on every startup, regardless of database/template/state content. Tested with zero templates, zero sandboxes, and CubeMaster stopped — all failed to mitigate.

## Root Cause

The `NewCubelet` function receives `rtManager runtemplate.RunTemplateManager` as a parameter. The `runtemplate` controller is registered at init time via `GetInMemorySandboxControllers()`, but its implementation fails the `CubeMetaController` interface check.

Source: `Cubelet/pkg/controller/runtemplate/template_manager.go`

Binary strings also reveal: `obj is not *templatetypes.LocalRunTemplate` and `failed to persist recovered local template`, suggesting a runtime type assertion failure.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Install Cube Sandbox v0.5.0 via one-click bare-metal installer
2. Start cubelet service
3. `systemctl status cube-sandbox-cubelet.service` shows `status=2/INVALIDARGUMENT` every ~5 minutes
4. Check `/data/log/Cubelet/Cubelet-req.log` for the FATAL entry

## Environment

- Cube Sandbox: v0.5.0 (30b4e25ab), also reproduced on v0.4.0 (4004a6ec)
- OS: Fedora 44, Linux 7.0.13, x86_64
- Filesystem: btrfs
- Installation: bare-metal one-click

## Impact

- Cubelet auto-restarts every ~5 minutes (systemd Restart=always)
- ~2-second service interruption per restart
- `cubecli exec` fails during crash windows
- Sandbox TAP networking requires reconnect after crash

## Attempted Mitigations (all failed)

- Deleting all template replicas/definitions from MySQL
- Deleting all cubelet state files and snapshots
- Stopping CubeMaster entirely
- Setting ReconcileInterval to 86400s
- Commenting out controller TOML config section
- Downgrading cubelet binary to v0.4.0
- seccomp filtering exit_group (caused SIGSYS crash)

## Log Snippet

```
{"LogLevel":"FATAL","LogContent":"controller run-template-manager is not a valid CubeMetaController"}
```
title: [Bug] Cubelet FATAL: controller run-template-manager is not a valid CubeMetaController

body:
## 【问题描述】
CubeSandbox 定位为面向 AI Agent 的安全沙箱服务，并与 e2b 协议兼容。Pi Agent是当前主流的终端型 AI 编码 Agent——它们在隔离环境中运行代码、编辑文件、执行命令，天然适合以 CubeSandbox 沙箱作为执行后端或运行环境：既可以把编码 Agent 本身跑在沙箱里获得隔离、可复现的运行环境，也可以让 Agent 编排系统按需拉起 CubeSandbox 沙箱执行其生成的代码。

在实际生产中，我们打算将 CubeSandbox 沙箱运用于 Pi Agent 的自进化Agentic RL 尝试中，目前 CubeSandbox 已有面向 OpenAI Agents、OpenClaw 等的集成示例，但尚未提供  Pi Agent 终端型编码 Agent 的集成文档与可运行示例。

## 【期望内容/功能改进】
1）为 Pi Agent 编写端到端集成指南，覆盖：在 CubeSandbox 中运行该 Agent 所需的模板构建、运行环境与依赖、API Key 等敏感配置的注入方式、网络与出口策略（Agent 需访问 LLM API）、以及会话保持与状态持久化（借助快照保存 Agent 运行状态、跨会话恢复）；
2）提供可运行的示例工程（置于 examples/ 下），包含模板定义与构建脚本、最小可复现的调用流程，以及能在本地部署环境跑通的 README；
3）给出典型使用场景与最佳实践：如把编码 Agent 跑在沙箱内做隔离开发、用沙箱执行 Agent 生成的代码并回收结果、利用快照实现 Agent 长时任务的断点续跑等；
4）补充常见问题与排错（鉴权失败、出口被拦截、镜像拉取、超时等），并与平台既有出口管控、鉴权、模板机制对齐；
5）文档纳入 docs/guide/integrations 体系，遵循既有集成文档模板与风格。

-----

## Problem Description

CubeSandbox is positioned as a secure sandbox service for AI Agents and is compatible with the e2b protocol. Pi Agent is a mainstream terminal-based AI coding Agent. It runs code, edits files, and executes commands in isolated environments, which makes it naturally suitable for using CubeSandbox as an execution backend or runtime environment.

CubeSandbox could support Pi Agent in two main ways:

1. Run the coding Agent itself inside a CubeSandbox environment to provide isolation and reproducible runtime conditions.
2. Allow an Agent orchestration system to launch CubeSandbox instances on demand to execute code generated by the Agent.

In our production scenario, we plan to use CubeSandbox for Pi Agent self-evolution and Agentic RL experiments. CubeSandbox already provides integration examples for OpenAI Agents, OpenClaw, and similar frameworks, but there is currently no integration documentation or runnable example for Pi Agent as a terminal-based coding Agent.

## Expected Feature / Improvement

I would like CubeSandbox to provide official documentation and examples for integrating with Pi Agent.

The integration should ideally include the following:

1. **End-to-end integration guide for Pi Agent**

   The guide should cover:

   * Template creation and build process required to run Pi Agent inside CubeSandbox.
   * Runtime environment and dependency setup.
   * Secure injection of sensitive configurations such as API keys.
   * Network and outbound access policies, since the Agent needs to access LLM APIs.
   * Session persistence and state recovery.
   * Using snapshots to save Agent runtime state and resume work across sessions.

2. **Runnable example project**

   Please provide a runnable example under the `examples/` directory, including:

   * Template definitions.
   * Build scripts.
   * A minimal reproducible invocation flow.
   * A README that can be followed in a local deployment environment.

3. **Typical use cases and best practices**

   The documentation should cover common scenarios such as:

   * Running the coding Agent inside a sandbox for isolated development.
   * Using CubeSandbox to execute code generated by the Agent and collect results.
   * Using snapshots to support checkpointing and resuming long-running Agent tasks.

4. **FAQ and troubleshooting**

   Please include troubleshooting guidance for common issues, such as:

   * Authentication failures.
   * Blocked outbound network access.
   * Image pull failures.
   * Timeout issues.
   * Problems related to platform authentication, outbound access control, and template mechanisms.

5. **Documentation placement and style**

   The documentation should be added under the existing `docs/guide/integrations` structure and follow the style and format of the existing integration documents.
title: [Feature Request] Integrate CubeSandbox with Pi Agent

body:
## Problem
Multiple clients call `CreateSandbox` concurrently. CubeMaster picks nodes using **cached metrics** (`MvmNum`, `QuotaCpuUsage`, `QuotaMemUsage`) with **no lock or reservation** at schedule time.
All concurrent requests can read the same stale snapshot, pass filters, and schedule onto the same node before metrics update.
## Flow (no lock)
```
CreateSandbox
  → scheduler.Select()     ← read MvmNum / quota from localcache (no lock)
  → callCubelet()
      → IncrNodeConcurrent()   ← only incremented here, after node is chosen
      → cubelet.Create()
  → metrics refresh on next heartbeat
```
- `preOccupy()` is empty — no reservation step.
- `IncrNodeConcurrent` runs **after** `Select()`, so filters never see in-flight creates.
- No Redis SETNX / per-node mutex / atomic reserve between "filter passed" and "cubelet accepted".
## Example
`node_max_mvm_num = 100`, node reports `MvmNum = 99`. Ten concurrent requests all see `99`, all pass prefilter, all schedule to the same node. No lock prevents this.
## Question
Should schedule-time **per-node locking or atomic reservation** be added before `callCubelet()`?
title: Concurrent CreateSandbox has no lock — scheduling race can oversell VMs

【产品名称/功能模块】
CubeSandbox 沙箱模板与示例生态

【问题描述】
一个沙箱平台的易用性，很大程度上取决于其开箱即用的模板与示例是否丰富——用户能否快速找到一个贴合自身场景的模板（某种语言运行时、数据科学环境、浏览器自动化、代码解释器、Web 开发环境、特定 Agent 框架的运行底座等）直接拉起沙箱，决定了上手成本。CubeSandbox 已具备从 OCI 镜像构建模板、快照、恢复等能力，并已有少量示例（如 code-sandbox-quickstart、browser-sandbox、mini-rl-training、openai-agents-example 等），但覆盖的场景与语言栈仍然有限，尚未形成系统化的模板/示例生态。

本 issue 为开放性生态贡献任务，目标是持续丰富 CubeSandbox 的模板与示例库，覆盖更多语言、框架与典型场景，让不同背景的开发者都能找到可直接复用的起点。允许多人并行参与、各自认领一个模板或示例，以增量方式合入，不要求单次提交完整 PR。

【期望内容/功能改进】（每人可认领其中一个或多个方向，渐进式贡献）
1）贡献一个或多个开箱即用的沙箱模板，覆盖但不限于：常见语言运行时（Python/Node/Go/Rust/Java 等）、数据科学与 ML（Jupyter、PyTorch、pandas 等）、浏览器自动化、代码解释器、Web 开发环境、特定 Agent 框架的运行底座等；
2）每个模板/示例应包含：模板定义与构建方式、最小可运行调用流程、README 说明（适用场景、资源建议、已知限制），并能在本地部署环境跑通；
3）鼓励覆盖差异化场景：长时任务与快照断点续跑、有状态工作区、多容器协作、出口网络策略受限下的运行等，体现 CubeSandbox 的差异化能力；
4）模板应遵循平台既有模板构建与命名约定，与出口管控、鉴权、资源限制等机制对齐，避免安全策略缺口；

**【Product Name / Feature Module】**
CubeSandbox Sandbox Templates & Example Ecosystem

**【Problem Description】**
A sandbox platform's usability depends heavily on how rich its out-of-the-box templates and examples are—whether users can quickly find a template that fits their scenario (a language runtime, data science environment, browser automation, code interpreter, web dev environment, runtime base for a specific Agent framework, etc.) and spin up a sandbox directly determines onboarding cost. CubeSandbox already supports building templates from OCI images, snapshots, restore, and similar capabilities, and has a few examples (e.g., code-sandbox-quickstart, browser-sandbox, mini-rl-training, openai-agents-example), but coverage of scenarios and language stacks is still limited and has not yet formed a systematic template/example ecosystem.

This issue is an open ecosystem contribution task aimed at continuously enriching CubeSandbox's template and example library, covering more languages, frameworks, and typical scenarios so developers from different backgrounds can find reusable starting points. Multiple contributors may participate in parallel, each claiming a template or example and merging incrementally—a single PR covering everything is not required.

**【Expected Content / Feature Improvements】** (Each contributor may claim one or more directions and contribute incrementally)
1) Contribute one or more out-of-the-box sandbox templates, covering but not limited to: common language runtimes (Python/Node/Go/Rust/Java, etc.), data science and ML (Jupyter, PyTorch, pandas, etc.), browser automation, code interpreters, web development environments, runtime bases for specific Agent frameworks, etc.;
2) Each template/example should include: template definition and build instructions, a minimal runnable workflow, README (use cases, resource recommendations, known limitations), and must work in a local deployment;
3) Encourage differentiated scenarios: long-running tasks with snapshot checkpoint/resume, stateful workspaces, multi-container collaboration, running under restricted egress policies, etc., showcasing CubeSandbox's differentiated capabilities;
4) Templates should follow the platform's existing template build and naming conventions, align with egress control, authentication, resource limits, and other mechanisms, and avoid security policy gaps;
5) Register in the `docs/guide/tutorials` or `examples` system with consistent style and easy discovery; this direction focuses on general language stacks/scenario templates, complementary to and non-overlapping with the "Claude Code / CodeBuddy / OpenCode Integration" direction.

**【Participation Guidelines & Acceptance】**
1) This is an open contribution: multiple people may claim different languages/frameworks/scenarios concurrently; contributions merge incrementally— no single person is expected to complete everything;
2) Each contribution should: build successfully and launch sandboxes, be reproducible, and have documentation consistent with current version behavior;
3) Minimum bar per contribution: at least one buildable template + runnable example + README, so others can follow the docs and get it working within a reasonable time;
4) Claim your specific direction in the issue comments to avoid duplicating existing examples or overlapping with others.

【产品名称/功能模块】
CubeSandbox WebUI 容器实例终端登录（Web Terminal）（PR合入类）

【问题描述】
CubeSandbox 的沙箱/容器实例运行在隔离环境中，开发者与运维人员经常需要"登录"进某个运行中的实例，进行调试、排查问题、手动安装依赖或执行临时命令。当前平台已提供命令执行能力，但 WebUI 上缺少一个交互式终端入口——用户无法在控制台直接打开一个 shell 进入指定实例，只能自行借助 CLI 或 SDK 拼接调用，使用体验割裂、上手成本高。

本 issue 希望在 CubeSandbox WebUI 上为运行中的沙箱/容器实例提供交互式终端登录能力，让用户在浏览器里即可获得一个完整的 shell 会话。

本 issue 为代码贡献任务，需阅读 CubeSandbox 现有代码（重点：沙箱命令执行相关能力、WebUI 前端工程、平台既有的 WebSocket 通道与鉴权机制），在本地虚拟机部署的 CubeSandbox 环境上完成开发与验证。

【期望内容/功能改进】
1）在 WebUI 的沙箱/容器实例列表或详情页，对运行中的实例提供"打开终端"入口，点击后弹出交互式终端面板；
2）终端基于成熟的 Web 终端组件实现，支持完整的交互式 shell 体验：输入输出、ANSI 颜色与光标控制、窗口尺寸自适应（resize）、复制粘贴、滚动回溯等；
3）后端提供基于 WebSocket 的交互式终端通道，将浏览器终端与实例的标准输入/输出/错误流双向打通，支持 TTY 模式与终端尺寸同步；应复用底层已有的容器执行/附着能力，不另起一套执行机制；
4）支持会话管理：终端会话的建立、保持、空闲超时与主动断开；异常断线时给出明确提示并支持重连；同一实例允许多开终端会话；
5）鉴权与访问控制：终端登录须经平台鉴权，仅授权用户可登录对应实例；校验目标实例存在且处于可登录状态（运行中），否则禁用入口并提示；记录终端会话的访问审计日志（操作人、时间、目标实例）；
6）支持多容器选择：一个沙箱包含多个容器时，可选择登录到指定容器；实例未运行或不可登录时给出清晰提示；
7）安全：终端通道沿用平台 HTTPS/WSS 加密传输；终端内可执行操作不超出实例既有权限边界，避免成为绕过出口/安全策略的通道；
8）用户体验与国际化：终端面板支持全屏、字号等基本设置（可选）；界面文案纳入 WebUI 既有多语言体系；
9）文档与示例：补充 WebUI 终端登录的使用说明、权限要求与已知限制；提供必要的截图或说明；
10）测试：补充后端通道的单元/集成测试（会话建立、鉴权、断开、尺寸同步）与前端终端组件的基本测试，提交 Pull Request 合入上游仓库。

【验收标准】
输出需具备如下功能：
1）WebUI 实例列表/详情页对运行中的沙箱/容器实例可见"打开终端"入口，点击后弹出交互式终端；
2）终端可成功登录目标实例，执行如 `ls`、`top`、`ping` 等命令，输入输出正常，ANSI 颜色与光标显示正确，且支持窗口 resize；
3）多个用户或多个实例可同时使用终端互不干扰，切换实例登录正确；
4）未授权用户无法登录；实例未运行时入口禁用并有提示；
5）终端会话支持主动断开与空闲超时，异常断线有明确提示；
6）终端登录行为有访问审计日志记录；
7）在本地 CubeSandbox 部署环境中，其他同学可依照文档在 30 分钟内从 WebUI 登录一个运行中的容器实例并执行命令；
8）单元/集成测试覆盖核心逻辑，PR 通过项目代码规范检查。

**【Product Name / Feature Module】**
CubeSandbox WebUI Container Instance Terminal Login (Web Terminal) (PR Merge Task)

**【Problem Description】**
CubeSandbox sandboxes/container instances run in isolated environments. Developers and operators often need to "log in" to a running instance for debugging, troubleshooting, manually installing dependencies, or running ad hoc commands. The platform already provides command execution capabilities, but the WebUI lacks an interactive terminal entry point—users cannot open a shell directly in the console to access a specific instance and must instead stitch together CLI or SDK calls on their own, resulting in a fragmented experience and a steep learning curve.

This issue aims to provide interactive terminal login for running sandboxes/container instances in the CubeSandbox WebUI, giving users a full shell session directly in the browser.

This issue is a code contribution task. You must read the existing CubeSandbox codebase (focus on sandbox command execution capabilities, the WebUI frontend project, and the platform's existing WebSocket channels and authentication mechanisms) and complete development and verification on a locally deployed CubeSandbox environment.

**【Expected Content / Feature Improvements】**
1) On the WebUI sandbox/container instance list or detail page, provide an "Open Terminal" entry for running instances; clicking it opens an interactive terminal panel;
2) Implement the terminal using a mature web terminal component, supporting a full interactive shell experience: input/output, ANSI colors and cursor control, window resize adaptation, copy/paste, scrollback, etc.;
3) The backend provides a WebSocket-based interactive terminal channel that bidirectionally connects the browser terminal to the instance's standard input/output/error streams, supporting TTY mode and terminal size synchronization; reuse the existing underlying container exec/attach capabilities rather than building a separate execution mechanism;
4) Support session management: terminal session establishment, keep-alive, idle timeout, and active disconnect; provide clear prompts on abnormal disconnect and support reconnection; allow multiple terminal sessions per instance;
5) Authentication and access control: terminal login must go through platform authentication; only authorized users may log in to the corresponding instance; verify that the target instance exists and is in a loggable state (running), otherwise disable the entry and show a prompt; record access audit logs for terminal sessions (operator, time, target instance);
6) Support multi-container selection: when a sandbox contains multiple containers, allow logging in to a specific container; provide clear prompts when the instance is not running or not loggable;
7) Security: the terminal channel uses the platform's existing HTTPS/WSS encrypted transport; operations executable within the terminal must not exceed the instance's existing permission boundaries, avoiding becoming a channel to bypass egress/security policies;
8) User experience and internationalization: the terminal panel supports basic settings such as fullscreen and font size (optional); UI text should be integrated into the WebUI's existing i18n system;
9) Documentation and examples: add usage instructions for WebUI terminal login, permission requirements, and known limitations; provide necessary screenshots or descriptions;
10) Testing: add unit/integration tests for the backend channel (session establishment, authentication, disconnect, size sync) and basic tests for the frontend terminal component; submit a Pull Request to merge into the upstream repository.

**【Acceptance Criteria】**
The deliverable must provide the following capabilities:
1) The WebUI instance list/detail page shows an "Open Terminal" entry for running sandboxes/container instances; clicking it opens an interactive terminal;
2) The terminal successfully logs in to the target instance; commands such as `ls`, `top`, and `ping` execute with normal input/output, correct ANSI colors and cursor display, and support window resize;
3) Multiple users or multiple instances can use terminals concurrently without interference; switching instances logs in correctly;
4) Unauthorized users cannot log in; when an instance is not running, the entry is disabled with a prompt;
5) Terminal sessions support active disconnect and idle timeout; abnormal disconnects show clear prompts;
6) Terminal login actions are recorded in access audit logs;
7) In a local CubeSandbox deployment, others can follow the documentation to log in to a running container instance from the WebUI and execute commands within 30 minutes;
8) Unit/integration tests cover core logic, and the PR passes the project's code quality checks.
